title: Pakistan’s LNG Imports Under Pressure: Impacts of the Strait of Hormuz’s Closure and Pakistan’s Diplomatic Response
gist: A five-month closure of the Strait of Hormuz and Qatar's Ras Laffan has slashed Pakistan's Qatar-dependent LNG imports, triggering blackouts and fertilizer-plant shutdowns; CSIS argues Pakistan could leverage its U.S.-Iran mediation and warming U.S. ties to secure U.S. LNG cargoes with EXIM credit support as the market tightens into winter.

insights.claim: The Strait of Hormuz and Qatar's Ras Laffan LNG export facility have been effectively shut for over five months due to the U.S.-Iran war, impacting 20 percent of the world's LNG supply.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A fifth of global LNG supply is offline, a major bullish shock to global gas prices and a stress test for import-dependent buyers.
insights.quote: impacting 20 percent of the world’s LNG supply

insights.claim: Over 90 percent of Pakistan's imported LNG comes from Qatar, and 7.5 of its 8.4 million tonnes per annum of active medium- and long-term contracts are from Qatari projects, leaving it acutely exposed to the Ras Laffan outage.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Extreme single-source concentration makes Pakistan the most exposed major Asian buyer and a forced spot-market participant.
insights.quote: with over 90 percent of their imported LNG coming from Qatar

insights.claim: Pakistan's LNG imports dropped 68 percent month-on-month and 69 percent year-on-year in March, while India and Bangladesh instead grew imports and diversified to U.S., Angola, Mozambique, Nigeria, Oman, and UAE cargoes.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Contrasting outcomes show diversification cushions supply shocks, underscoring Pakistan's vulnerability from Qatar concentration.
insights.quote: its LNG imports in March dropping 68 percent month-on-month and 69 percent year-on-year
insights.locator: Pakistan’s LNG Purchases and Changing Energy Mix

insights.claim: Pakistan's post-Covid financial crisis brought it near sovereign default with inflation hitting a record 38 percent in 2023, and its non-investment-grade credit rating and IMF austerity make long-term LNG contracts more expensive via seller risk premiums.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Weak sovereign credit structurally raises Pakistan's cost of securing LNG, limiting its ability to lock in supply.
insights.quote: make signing long-term contracts more expensive due to risk premiums added by sellers to protect themselves against the buyer defaulting
insights.locator: Pakistan’s LNG Purchases and Changing Energy Mix

insights.claim: Traditionally price-sensitive buyers Bangladesh, India, and Pakistan are now paying spot LNG in the low $20s per MMBtu—India recently over $23—versus $12-13 in May-June 2025, with Pakistan buying a mid-July cargo at $21.88/MMBtu.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A roughly 70 percent spot-price jump quantifies the demand-destruction pressure on South Asian buyers and margin for exporters.
insights.quote: now purchasing spot cargoes in the lower $20s per million British thermal units (MMBtu) of LNG
insights.locator: Pakistan’s LNG Purchases and Changing Energy Mix

insights.claim: Pakistan shifted its March-April 2026 power mix to roughly 30 percent coal and just 4-6 percent LNG, versus a five-year average near 20 percent each, yet still suffered planned blackouts.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Fuel-switching to coal cushioned but could not offset the LNG loss, showing the limits of Pakistan's substitution options.
insights.quote: coal usage rise to around 30 percent and much lower power generation from LNG imports—between 4–6 percent
insights.locator: Pakistan’s LNG Purchases and Changing Energy Mix

insights.claim: Pakistan shut two fertilizer plants to redirect gas to power, and Sui Northern Gas Pipelines issued a force majeure suspending supply to Agritech's 433k-tonne-per-year urea plant, threatening fertilizer during rice transplanting and wheat sowing seasons.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Gas rationing is cascading into agricultural output risk, a food-security and inflation channel beyond electricity.
insights.quote: Pakistan has shut two fertilizer plants to redirect gas to the power sector because of tighter LNG supplies

insights.claim: A strong El Niño pattern this autumn is expected to bring hotter, drier weather that could cut water for hydropower and nuclear reactors, driving Pakistan's demand for LNG and coal even higher.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Weather risk compounds the supply squeeze, raising the chance of deeper energy shortfalls into winter.

insights.claim: QatarEnergy has extended its LNG force majeure through September, is preparing to extend into October, and has leased out LNG tankers through mid-October despite low freight rates, signaling its own expectation of a delayed Ras Laffan restart.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Qatar's own tanker leasing behavior is a bearish supply tell that the outage will persist, prolonging the price spike.
insights.quote: has tellingly leased out some of its LNG tankers through mid-October despite lower freight rates, signaling its own expectations of Ras Laffan’s delayed startup timeline

insights.claim: Europe is ending its gas injection season at levels similar to post-2023 and will likely re-enter the spot market, driving LNG prices higher just as Pakistan competes for winter cargoes.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: European restocking demand tightens the global market further, intensifying competition and price pressure for weaker buyers.
insights.quote: it will therefore likely be reentering the spot market and driving up LNG prices in the coming weeks and months

insights.claim: An estimated 79 percent of Qatar's state revenues come from LNG, revenues used to assert independence from Saudi Arabia, fund Al-Jazeera, and build U.S. university ties, so its passage-dependence on Iran's approval is a strategic vulnerability.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Highlights how the Hormuz chokepoint threatens the fiscal base of a key U.S. Gulf partner, a geopolitical fragility.
insights.quote: An estimated 79 percent of Qatar’s state revenues...come from LNG

insights.claim: CSIS argues Pakistan could leverage its U.S.-Iran mediation role and improving U.S. ties to procure U.S. LNG cargoes, with the U.S. providing cost subsidies and EXIM credit support so Pakistan can tender for U.S. LNG.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Points to a potential U.S.-backed opening for American LNG exporters to develop the Pakistani market via government credit support.
insights.quote: the United States could facilitate the sale of U.S. LNG cargoes to Pakistan to cover its energy shortfall through the crisis

insights.claim: An early-July Iranian attack on a Qatari LNG tanker attempting the strait shows Qatar's ability to ship cargoes now depends on the end buyer's relationship with Iran, making passage a function of diplomatic skill rather than commercial contract.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Delivery risk is now politically contingent, a novel form of supply uncertainty buyers and insurers must price.
insights.quote: Qatar’s ability to send cargoes through the strait depends on the end buyer’s negotiating skills and relationship with Iran
